title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models
authors: Aravindan Kamatchi Sundaram, B. Pabitramohan Prusty, Rohit Batra
abstract: Over the past decade, substantial efforts have been devoted to developing machine learning (ML) methods for extracting materials data and, where possible, materials knowledge directly from the scientific literature. This review traces the evolution of these methods from heuristic, rule-based pipelines through natural language processing (NLP) models and transformer-based encoders to, lastly, large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems capable of extracting materials information across multiple modalities, including text, tables, and figures. Beside construction of large, queryable materials databases and knowledge graphs that support downstream materials discovery, we discuss how these advances have enabled new capabilities, such as, generic question answering across materials science, AI co-scientists and chatbots for research assistance, and closed-loop optimization and discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories. We critically assess the datasets generated using these approaches, their extraction accuracy and computational costs, and the respective strengths and limitations of different methodologies, and even provide practical guidelines for developing more reliable and scalable materials data extraction pipelines. Finally, we identify key open challenges, including the extraction of full materials structure-property-processing-performance tetrahedron at the sample level, the scarcity of reliable benchmark datasets for systematic evaluation, and the resolution of non-standard materials terminology across different document modalities.

infographic.key_insight: This review traces how materials information extraction has evolved from rule-based pipelines to multimodal LLMs and agentic systems supporting materials discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automated literature extraction can populate materials databases and knowledge graphs, support research assistants, and enable closed-loop discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories.
method: Review rule-based, NLP, transformer, and LLM extraction approaches.
Examine extraction across text, tables, and figures.
Assess generated datasets, extraction accuracy, computational costs, and pipeline reliability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a critical assessment of datasets and extraction methods but reports no numerical performance results and identifies a shortage of reliable evaluation benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Reliable sample-level linkage of structure, properties, processing, and performance remains an open challenge, compounded by inconsistent terminology across document modalities.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models

title: Vacancy-enhanced Li solid-solution anodes for solid-state batteries: computational screening enabling high critical current density
authors: Arseniy S. Burov, Nadezhda A. Ashikhmina, Nurlan Zhanabayev, Anton O. Boev, Aleksandra D. Radina, Ilya V. Chepkasov
abstract: Sluggish vacancy-mediated self-diffusion in lithium metal limits the critical current density (CCD) of Li anodes in solid-state batteries by promoting interfacial void formation during stripping. To enhance the effective vacancy concentration while preserving the bcc Li host, we screen 50 substitutional solutes using density functional theory (DFT) within a funnel based on automatic phase diagram construction, solution energies, solute-vacancy binding energies, and experimental solubility limits. Using an adaptation of the Lomer model for the dilute limit, we show that only Ag, Ge, and Cd solid solutions are predicted to reach $1~\mathrm{mA~cm^{-2}}$ within their solubility limits. The thermodynamically estimated CCD of Ag at $\sim 9$ at.% reaches $\sim 4~\mathrm{mA~cm^{-2}}$ at a theoretical capacity of $1522~\mathrm{mAh~g^{-1}}$. Migration barrier calculations indicate that the enhancement may be partially offset by vacancy trapping, necessitating further validation via molecular dynamics simulations. Notably, Hume-Rothery rules alone prove insufficient as prefilters, whereas machine-learning models trained on the DFT data can eliminate most unsuitable solutes early in the funnel and extend the workflow to related solid-solution searches.

infographic.key_insight: Screening 50 solutes predicts that Ag, Ge, and Cd can enhance vacancy-mediated transport in bcc Li enough to reach 1 mA cm⁻² within their solubility limits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Li–Ag at approximately 9 at.% Ag has a thermodynamically estimated critical current density of approximately 4 mA cm⁻² while retaining a theoretical capacity of 1522 mAh g⁻¹.
method: DFT screening using automated phase diagrams, solution energies, solute–vacancy binding energies, and experimental solubility limits.
Adapted dilute-limit Lomer model to estimate vacancy enhancement and critical current density.
Migration-barrier calculations and DFT-trained machine learning to assess trapping and accelerate solute filtering.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 50 screened solutes, only Ag, Ge, and Cd were predicted to reach the 1 mA cm⁻² target within their solubility limits; Hume–Rothery rules alone were insufficient as prefilters.
infographic.watch_item: Vacancy trapping may partly offset the predicted enhancement, requiring further validation through molecular dynamics simulations.
infographic.paper_title: Vacancy-enhanced Li solid-solution anodes for solid-state batteries: computational screening enabling high critical current density

title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery
authors: Yazhuo Liu, Kunqing Ding, Xiaoguo Gong, Zifeng Wang, Yichen Yang, Yifeng Che
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.

infographic.key_insight: GBClaw connects agentic AI workflows with atomistic simulations to reveal how defect hierarchies and metastable grain-boundary structures influence sliding resistance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could help researchers investigate interface-controlled deformation and inform microstructure design in polycrystalline materials.
method: Coordinate LLMs, specialized agents, domain tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory.
Dynamically replan simulations and refine workflows for targeted mechanistic analysis.
Compare boundary sliding with and without secondary misfit dislocations, then perform researcher-guided follow-up calculations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 14 general asymmetric tilt grain boundaries in nickel, GBClaw identified diverse deformation modes and substantial shear-strength differences associated with secondary misfit dislocations.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to the studied nickel boundaries, and resolving anomalous behavior required researcher-guided follow-up.
infographic.paper_title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery

title: Microstructural Generative Inverse Models for Additive Manufacturing Digital Twins
authors: Pablo Luna Falcon, Jason Mayeur, Amirkoushyar Ziabari, Vincent Paquit, Patxi Fernandez-Zelaia
abstract: Metal additive manufacturing (AM) offers substantial advantages to the fabrication of complex structural components, but its widespread adoption is slowed due to complexities in the process-structure-property relations which is the cause for uncertainty and drives risk. Accurately quantifying these complex relations solely via experimental workflows is time consuming and costly. Integrated computational materials and engineering (ICME) frameworks address this challenge by leveraging advanced computational tools, such as crystal plasticity finite element models (CPFEM), to predict critical mechanical properties directly from microstructural data. However, these frameworks require a large datasets that are often difficult to obtain, and their predictive accuracy depends on the availability of realistic AM microstructure representations. Generative deep learning models are a promising approach towards synthesizing AM microstructures which contain complex morphological and crystallographic features. Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), in particular, show a strong potential to capture the inherent complexities of AM structures. In this work, we demonstrate that DDPMs can reliably synthesize digital-twin orientation-imaging micrographs, and we support this claim with quantitative evidence of the fidelity of the generated samples. Additionally, we establish a classifier-free guidance framework for solving complex inverse problems such as property-to-structure and process-to-structure mappings, and we showcase a potential application on a qualification-relevant uncertainty quantification problem. Our work highlights the potential of AI-based generative modeling as a key component of computational frameworks for accelerating AM materials qualification and certification.

infographic.key_insight: Denoising diffusion models synthesize realistic additive-manufacturing orientation micrographs and enable property-to-structure and process-to-structure inverse mappings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Synthetic microstructures could support computational digital twins and help accelerate metal additive-manufacturing qualification while reducing reliance on costly experiments.
method: Use denoising diffusion probabilistic models to generate microstructural orientation images.
Apply classifier-free guidance to condition generation on properties or processing information.
Demonstrate a qualification-relevant uncertainty quantification application.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports quantitative evidence of generated-sample fidelity, but provides no dataset sizes, evaluation metrics, or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Micrograph fidelity alone does not establish reliable downstream mechanical predictions or generalization across additive-manufacturing conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Microstructural Generative Inverse Models for Additive Manufacturing Digital Twins

title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation
authors: Ouns El Harzli, Jelle Bor, Linde Wester, Leonid Zhukov, Hanl Park, Jean-François Bobier
abstract: We develop an end-to-end framework for assessing a quantum-computing application in industrial materials science: the screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for SOFCs and SOECs. We formulate the materials problem in terms of interface observables including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. We describe how these observables can be obtained using a diagrammatic GW-based embedding, either GW+DMFT or self-energy embedding theory (SEET), applied to a DFT-screened shortlist. The atomistic electrode/electrolyte interface defines the electronic structure problem from which the correlated impurity models are constructed. Quantum impurity solvers would provide the finite-temperature impurity Green's functions required by the embedding. The computational challenges that classical solvers may encounter as the interacting active space grows, together with the polynomial scaling of quantum Hamiltonian simulation for efficiently represented discretized models, open an opportunity for quantum advantage. We identify the benchmarks needed to assess this opportunity through convergence of vacancy and migration energetics and comparison with the best applicable classical solvers. We provide illustrative logical qubit counts and identify the thermal state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated-solve costs needed for a complete resource assessment. We connect microscopic observables to macroscopic engineering metrics using a continuum model for mixed ionic--electronic conducting oxygen electrodes that couples oxygen surface exchange, solid-state oxygen transport, electrode microstructure, and finite electrode thickness. Finally, we estimate the potential worldwide business value of improved electrode materials under SOFC and SOEC deployment scenarios informed by public technical targets and electrolyser deployment data.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum impurity solvers could enable more accurate screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for solid oxide fuel and electrolysis cells.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework links interface energetics and conductivity to electrode performance through oxygen exchange, transport, microstructure, and thickness.
method: Screen candidate materials with DFT and construct correlated impurity models from electrode–electrolyte interfaces.
Use GW+DMFT or SEET embedding with quantum solvers for finite-temperature impurity Green’s functions.
Connect microscopic observables to continuum electrode models and deployment-based business-value estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract provides illustrative logical-qubit counts and proposes benchmarks based on converged vacancy and migration energetics and comparisons with leading applicable classical solvers.
infographic.watch_item: Quantum advantage remains unproven; full resource estimates must include thermal-state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated solves.
infographic.paper_title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation

title: Multiscale Modeling of Zr Corrosion: Predicting Microstructures of Oxide Films
authors: K. Starkey, L. Kahle, M. Christensen, V. Eyert, A. El-Azab, C. B. Geller
abstract: A first-principles-informed multiscale modeling approach is reported for oxide formation during corrosion of zirconium. The present simulations reproduce the columnar corrosion film microstructure and grain size distribution seen in micrographs of oxidized Zr surfaces. This structural feature emerges from a hexagonal ZrO layer adjacent to the $α$-Zr/ZrO$_{2-x}$ interface, which is dynamically stabilized by continuous heterogeneous grain nucleation and grain boundary mass diffusion. This ZrO layer is identified as a significant oxygen diffusion barrier and a potential contributor to sub-parabolic pretransition corrosion kinetics. The simulations also reproduce the undulatory nature of the metal/oxide interface, leading to regions with tensile stress components capable of nucleating cracks, despite the overall state of compressive hydrostatic stress within the oxide film. First principles density functional theory (DFT) computations of fundamental ZrO$_x$ properties were combined with molecular dynamics simulations using a machine-learned potential based on a DFT training set to provide extensive input to an advanced phase field model for oxide formation and its microstructure, as implemented in the new MedeA PhaseField module. The phase field simulations reported herein incorporated computed stoichiometry-dependent thermochemical data, anisotropic elastic properties, interface energies, bulk and grain boundary mass transport processes, multiphase heterogeneous grain nucleation, and strain energy-dependent phase stabilities.

infographic.key_insight: Multiscale simulations identify a dynamically stabilized hexagonal ZrO interlayer as a key driver of columnar oxide microstructure and a significant oxygen diffusion barrier during zirconium corrosion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predicting oxide morphology, oxygen transport, and local tensile stresses could help assess zirconium corrosion and crack initiation.
method: Compute ZrOₓ thermochemistry and material properties using density functional theory.
Use molecular dynamics with a DFT-trained machine-learned potential to supply additional model inputs.
Simulate oxide growth in MedeA PhaseField with heterogeneous nucleation, mass transport, and elastic effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations reproduce columnar oxide morphology and grain size distributions seen in micrographs, as well as an undulatory metal/oxide interface.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative validation metrics, and the proposed link between the ZrO barrier and sub-parabolic corrosion kinetics remains tentative.
infographic.paper_title: Multiscale Modeling of Zr Corrosion: Predicting Microstructures of Oxide Films

title: Rationalizing charge transfer: a single-molecule case study across three distinct surfaces
authors: Benjamin Lowe, Jan Berger, Martin Ondráček, Oleksandr Stetsovych, Shayan Louie, Marco Lozano
abstract: Organic molecules are versatile building blocks for the formation of complex low-dimensional nanostructures on surfaces. Recently, interest has grown in translating on-surface synthetic protocols from noble metal surfaces to insulating surfaces, which offer technological relevance, and to magnetic or superconducting surfaces, which offer new routes to correlated phases. It is important, therefore, to understand how these alternative surfaces may alter the properties of adsorbates through processes like charge transfer and screening. Evidence for charge transfer is often obtained experimentally via scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS), and theoretically via density functional theory (DFT). In this work, we systematically compare the properties of isolated macrocyclic emeraldine (Me$_6$) molecules on three different surfaces: metallic Au(111), a semiconducting ferromagnetic monolayer of FeCl$_2$, and a cleaved superconducting surface of bulk 2H-NbSe$_2$. We show that STS and DFT alone are insufficient to quantify charge transfer for these cases. Instead, we complement these methods with Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) measurements and model Hamiltonian calculations to demonstrate that on Au(111) and FeCl$_2$, Me$_6$ molecules donate a single electron to the substrate, whereas on NbSe$_2$ two electrons are transferred from molecule to substrate. Our work provides insight into the interplay of charge transfer, screening, and molecule-substrate coupling, and develops experimental and theoretical methods for comparing the properties of adsorbates across different surfaces for future studies.

infographic.key_insight: Isolated macrocyclic emeraldine (Me₆) molecules donate one electron to Au(111) and FeCl₂, but two electrons to 2H-NbSe₂.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding substrate-dependent charge transfer can guide the design of molecular nanostructures on metallic, magnetic, and superconducting surfaces.
method: Compare isolated Me₆ molecules across three distinct substrates.
Combine scanning tunneling spectroscopy and density functional theory with Kelvin probe force microscopy.
Use model Hamiltonian calculations to interpret charge transfer and screening.
infographic.evidence_signal: Combined measurements and calculations distinguish single-electron donation on Au(111) and FeCl₂ from two-electron donation on NbSe₂.
infographic.watch_item: STS and DFT alone cannot quantify charge transfer in these systems; complementary measurements and modeling are needed.
infographic.paper_title: Rationalizing charge transfer: a single-molecule case study across three distinct surfaces

title: Side-Chain Engineering Controls Molecular Packing and Vertical Electron Transport in Discrete n-Type NDI-T2 Oligomers
authors: Zihao Liu, Hajar Komekoz, Nisarg Trivedi, Max Dorfner, Lokesh Rasabathina, Rico Ehrler
abstract: High-efficiency vertical charge transport in multilayer organic optoelectronic devices highly depends on molecular structure and arrangement. Using two T2-(NDI-T2)2 conjugated oligomers with ethylhexyl (EH) and octyldodecyl (OD) side chains as a model system, their effects on electron transport are investigated using, among other techniques, atomic force microscopy (AFM), conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM), grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS), steady-state optical spectroscopy, and time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) calculations. The oligomers of both materials exhibit relatively disordered structures in the as-cast state, whereas annealing enhances structural order and leads to side-chain-dependent changes in molecular stacking. EH-based films show a smaller annealing-induced photoluminescence shift than OD-based films, suggesting less pronounced stacking and conformational rearrangements, consistent with TDDFT-supported exciton analysis. The current-voltage characteristics are analyzed using the space-charge-limited current (SCLC) model. After annealing, both materials exhibit improved vertical electron mobility. The EH-based films reach a maximum mobility of 1.2 x 10^-4 cm^2 V^-1 s^-1. The combined results suggest that the shorter EH side chains modify the out-of-plane packing environment and facilitate vertical electron transport. These results establish a structure-property relationship between side-chain structure, molecular order, exciton coupling and vertical mobility, providing a molecular design basis for optimising organic semiconductors through side-chain engineering.

infographic.key_insight: Side-chain engineering controls annealing-induced packing changes in NDI-T2 oligomers, with shorter ethylhexyl chains supporting improved vertical electron transport.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tuning side-chain length and thermal processing offers a molecular design strategy for improving electron transport through multilayer organic optoelectronic devices.
method: Compare ethylhexyl- and octyldodecyl-substituted oligomer films before and after annealing.
Probe morphology, packing and optical response using AFM, GIWAXS and steady-state spectroscopy, supported by TDDFT.
Measure vertical conduction with C-AFM and extract mobility using a space-charge-limited current model.
infographic.evidence_signal: Annealing improved vertical electron mobility in both materials; ethylhexyl-based films reached a maximum of 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ and showed a smaller photoluminescence shift than octyldodecyl-based films.
infographic.watch_item: Mobility estimates depend on SCLC model assumptions, and performance in complete multilayer devices is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Side-Chain Engineering Controls Molecular Packing and Vertical Electron Transport in Discrete n-Type NDI-T2 Oligomers

title: Unifying Low-Frequency Raman and Infrared Signatures across Perovskites
authors: Ethan Berger, Erik Fransson, Apinya Ngoipala, Lucas Svensson, Priyanka Deswal, Mehmet Baskurt
abstract: Perovskites have been studied for a wide range of applications, from oxide-based ferroelectrics to halide-perovskite photovoltaics. Despite their diverse functionalities, these materials share strong lattice anharmonicity arising from structural instabilities such as polar off-centering and octahedral tilting. These anharmonic distortions strongly influence the low-frequency vibrational response and can be observed in infrared (IR) and Raman spectra. However, low-frequency IR and Raman signatures are typically investigated separately, hindering the development of a unified understanding of vibrational spectroscopy across perovskite classes. In this work, we use machine-learning-based molecular dynamics to simulate the IR and Raman spectra of oxide perovskites (SrTiO$_3$ and BaTiO$_3$), halide perovskites (CsPbBr$_3$, CsSnBr$_3$, and CsGeBr$_3$) and double halide perovskites (Cs$_2$AgAlBr$_6$ and Cs$_2$AgBiBr$_6$). By comparing materials exhibiting polar, tilt-driven and mixed instabilities, we find that polar off-centering leads to enhanced low-frequency IR and dielectric responses, whereas nonpolar modes, particularly octahedral tilting, are associated with Raman central peaks. The strength of the low-frequency features also depends on how strongly the underlying modes couple to polarization or dielectric susceptibility. Finally, we show that the dynamics of these instabilities play an important role, with slow polar reorientations shifting the dielectric response to very low frequencies and overdamped tilting modes producing persistent Raman central peaks. These results establish a unified framework connecting low-frequency IR and Raman spectra to the symmetry, coupling and dynamics of their underlying anharmonic lattice instabilities.

infographic.key_insight: Across perovskites, polar off-centering enhances low-frequency infrared and dielectric responses, while nonpolar octahedral tilting is associated with Raman central peaks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Linking spectral features to lattice-instability symmetry, coupling and dynamics can guide interpretation of perovskite behavior relevant to ferroelectric and photovoltaic materials.
method: Simulate infrared and Raman spectra using machine-learning-based molecular dynamics.
Compare seven oxide, halide and double-halide perovskites with polar, tilt-driven or mixed instabilities.
Relate low-frequency features to polarization or dielectric-susceptibility coupling and instability dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations across seven compositions show that slow polar reorientations shift dielectric response to very low frequencies, while overdamped tilting modes produce persistent Raman central peaks.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no quantitative experimental validation or model-accuracy metrics, limiting assessment of predictive reliability.
infographic.paper_title: Unifying Low-Frequency Raman and Infrared Signatures across Perovskites

title: First-principles modeling of ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys
authors: Daniil M. Khodachenko, Andrei V. Ruban, Franco Moitzi, Oleg E. Peil, Vsevolod I. Razumovskiy
abstract: The atomic ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys strongly influences their magnetic properties and mechanical behavior. While general features of long-range atomic ordering are known from the experimentally established phase diagram in this composition range, detailed atomic configurations and driving forces behind them remain speculative. Here, we address this gap by using effective cluster interactions (ECI) obtained from density functional theory (DFT) calculations and subsequent statistical thermodynamics modeling to unravel the interplay between magnetism, composition, and temperature in body-centered cubic (bcc) Fe-Si alloys up to 20 at% Si. Our analysis reveals that the ordering behavior is governed by a strong coupling between magnetic order, lattice expansion, and Si concentration, with specific ECI shells switching sign or magnitude as the magnetic state changes, which is reflected in the phase equilibria and ordering behavior of Fe-Si alloys. In particular, we demonstrate that D0$_3$ ordering is, in fact, primary in the totally ordered ferromagnetic state, while the B2 type of ordering is promoted in the paramagnetic state at elevated temperatures. The temperature-dependent evolution of these ordering patterns, obtained from Monte Carlo simulations based on the magnetically resolved ECIs, reproduces the experimentally observed phase equilibria and short-range order characteristics. By explicitly linking the magnetic state with the effective interactions and macroscopic phase behavior, this work establishes a predictive framework for an ab initio-based description of ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys and highlights the decisive role of magnetism in ordering phenomena in this system.

infographic.key_insight: Magnetism controls ordering in Fe-rich Fe–Si alloys: D0₃ ordering dominates in the fully ordered ferromagnetic state, while B2 ordering is promoted in the high-temperature paramagnetic state.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Linking magnetic state to atomic ordering can help guide composition and thermal-processing choices for Fe–Si alloys whose magnetic and mechanical behavior depends on atomic arrangement.
method: Calculate effective cluster interactions using density functional theory.
Resolve how magnetic state, lattice expansion, and Si concentration affect interactions.
Use Monte Carlo simulations to predict temperature-dependent ordering in bcc alloys up to 20 at% Si.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulated ordering evolution reproduces experimentally observed phase equilibria and short-range order characteristics, although the abstract reports no quantitative agreement metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The demonstrated scope is bcc Fe–Si alloys up to 20 at% Si; extrapolation to other compositions or structures requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: First-principles modeling of ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys

title: STAR-XPC: Set Transformer for Estimating X-ray Transmission in Polymer Composites
authors: Can Erer, H. Birkan Yilmaz, Nebahat Aral
abstract: Evaluating the energy transmission ratio of an X-ray beam through a polymer composite is a challenging task in radiation shielding studies. The reference solution with Monte Carlo transport simulation is highly accurate but computationally expensive: each of our reference simulations is capped at $4\times10^9$ photon histories and a 20,000 s (over 5 hours) time limit, while closed-form analytical methods fail to represent such complex scenarios. We present an artificial neural network model that maps the unordered multi-set of molecular constituents, their mass fractions, and four bulk physical descriptors directly to the transmission ratio $I(t)/I_0$ in 1-3 milliseconds. The model is a Set Transformer, which makes it permutation invariant by construction and accepts mixtures of different sizes up to 11 constituents within a fixed-size padded set. Each constituent is embedded with a chemistry-pretrained transformer language model, ChemBERTa. In our proposed method, training data are produced by an automated PENELOPE/penEasy pipeline using the radiation source at 30, 80, 100, and 120 kV tube voltages over polyethylene-based shielding composite slabs of thicknesses spanning 0.15-2.5 mm. After preprocessing, the dataset contains $n = 4697$ simulated configurations on which a leakage-free, jointly stratified 10-fold cross-validation is performed, attaining mean squared error MSE = $(1.12 \pm 0.56)\times10^{-4}$, normalized-MSE percentage NMSE% = 0.0294% $\pm$ 0.0147%, and $R^2 = 0.9988$. The corresponding per-sample percentage errors give an alpha-trimmed ($α= 0.10$) absolute percentage error (APE) of 1.66% and a median APE of 1.15%. Our model's inference is several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying Monte Carlo simulation (sub-millisecond per query vs. several hours for the reference run) with effective accuracy in predicting $I(t)/I_0$.

infographic.key_insight: STAR-XPC predicts X-ray transmission through polymer composites in milliseconds, closely matching computationally expensive Monte Carlo reference simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model could accelerate screening of polyethylene-based radiation shields across composition, thickness, and X-ray tube voltage.
method: Encode molecular constituents with pretrained ChemBERTa embeddings and include their mass fractions.
Use a permutation-invariant Set Transformer for mixtures of up to 11 constituents plus four bulk physical descriptors.
Train on transmission ratios generated by an automated PENELOPE/penEasy simulation pipeline.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 4,697 simulated configurations, leakage-free, jointly stratified 10-fold cross-validation achieved R² = 0.9988 and median absolute percentage error = 1.15%.
infographic.watch_item: Performance outside the studied polyethylene-based composites, 0.15–2.5 mm thicknesses, and four tube voltages—and agreement with physical experiments—remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: STAR-XPC: Set Transformer for Estimating X-ray Transmission in Polymer Composites

title: Probing the limits of forward screening and inverse design of crystal materials
authors: Zhilong Song, Zijun Pang, Lixue Cheng
abstract: Crystal materials are designed either by screening known crystals for a target property or by generating new crystals with that property. Both routes are judged against public databases of known crystals, but these databases name the same crystal differently. Several materials announced as new by recent generative and autonomous discovery campaigns have since proved to be known phases or close variants of them. The limits of both routes remain unmeasured. Here we probe them by matching the crystals of 55 databases by structure into one self-extending database of 14.6 million crystals and 131.8 million property values, each traced to its source. Only 4.5% of its crystal-property pairs carry a value. To fill the empty pairs, we developed CGTNet, an equivariant graph transformer with state-of-the-art accuracy on several tasks of two public benchmarks. Trained on each task, it forms a library of property models whose predictions we release. The reach of forward screening has been underestimated. Known crystals hold tens of thousands of ultra-incompressible candidates without a recorded bulk modulus, and a post hoc audit of synthesis evidence finds among them ReN2, whose bulk modulus was measured at 428 GPa. The novelty claimed for inverse design has been overestimated. At an equal verification budget, a stiffness-conditioned generator returned more stiff hits than screening (100 versus 55), but all contained osmium and 82 repeated recorded compositions. Integrating and completing the databases of known crystals therefore moves the limits of both routes: it widens what screening can reach and sets the reference against which generated crystals are judged new.

infographic.key_insight: Unifying known-crystal databases expands forward screening opportunities while revealing that inverse-designed materials may be less novel than claimed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can search overlooked known crystals for target properties and assess generated candidates against a broader, structure-matched reference.
method: Match crystal structures across 55 databases, retaining source provenance.
Train CGTNet, an equivariant graph transformer, to predict missing material properties.
Compare screening and stiffness-conditioned generation at equal verification budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: The integrated database contains 14.6 million crystals and 131.8 million property values; generation produced 100 stiff hits versus screening’s 55, but all generated hits contained osmium and 82 repeated recorded compositions.
infographic.watch_item: Only 4.5% of crystal–property pairs have recorded values, so model predictions require validation and novelty checks must go beyond composition alone.
infographic.paper_title: Probing the limits of forward screening and inverse design of crystal materials

title: Nitrogen vacancy cluster-mediated ferroelectric domain growth in wurtzite AlN
authors: Zijian Zhou, Kan-Hao Xue, Ziqi Pang, Heng Yu, Shanzhong Xie, Hang Liu
abstract: Aluminum nitride-based ferroelectrics combine high remanent polarization, thermal stability, weak size effects, a wide bandgap and back-end process compatibility, making them promising for high density non-volatile memory. However, their high coercive field ($E_\mathrm{c}$) and unclear polarization switching mechanism limit further applications. Theoretical predictions indicate preferential reversed domain growth along the polar axis, whereas experiments show nearly isotropic growth or preferential growth perpendicular to this axis. Here, we combine density functional theory, Deep Potential molecular dynamics and experimental characterization to determine how nitrogen vacancies ($V_\mathrm{N}$) regulate domain growth and $E_\mathrm{c}$. In ideal crystal, strong lattice coupling along the polar axis drives preferential domain growth in this direction. $V_\mathrm{N}$ locally weakens this coupling and promotes polarization nucleation. The spatial distribution of $V_\mathrm{N}$ and the temporal sequence of vacancy induced switching jointly determine the direction and morphology of reversed domain growth. We further show that scandium doping promotes $V_\mathrm{N}$ formation, thereby enhancing defect mediated nucleation and reducing $E_\mathrm{c}$. These findings establish a multiscale mechanism governing thin-film domain-growth kinetics and macroscopic $E_\mathrm{c}$, reconciling experimental observations with ideal crystal simulations and providing defect engineering principles for low-voltage, reliable and scalable ferroelectric devices.

infographic.key_insight: Nitrogen vacancies weaken polar-axis lattice coupling in wurtzite AlN, enabling defect-mediated switching whose spatial and temporal patterns govern ferroelectric domain growth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineering nitrogen-vacancy distributions, aided by scandium doping, offers a route to lower coercive fields for low-voltage ferroelectric memory.
method: Density functional theory calculations
Deep Potential machine-learning molecular dynamics
Experimental characterization
infographic.evidence_signal: Combined simulations and experimental characterization support vacancy-mediated nucleation and reconcile ideal-crystal predictions of polar-axis growth with experimentally observed lateral or nearly isotropic growth.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify the vacancy-control window or device-level reliability trade-offs needed to translate reduced coercive fields into scalable memory.
infographic.paper_title: Nitrogen vacancy cluster-mediated ferroelectric domain growth in wurtzite AlN

title: Universal Synthesis of Large-Area Hybrid Perovskite Monolayers Enabling Lithography-Free, Low-Static-Power Optoelectronics
authors: Shankeerthan Kalyanasundaram, Swarit Dwivedi, Sanje Mahasivam, Christopher R. McNeill, Sudha Mokkapati
abstract: Solution-phase synthesis of monolayer hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites is constrained by rapid out-of-plane crystal growth, uncontrolled nucleation, and strong interlayer aggregation, yielding flakes of only a few μm. We introduce a steric-engineering ternary-solvent growth strategy to synthesize monolayer and few-layer A2MX4 hybrid perovskites with exceptionally large surface areas. By combining alcohol cosolvents with an amine additive, out-of-plane stacking is suppressed. Using (PEA)2CuCl4 as a model system, monolayers with lateral areas exceeding 1000 μm2 are achieved, representing a massive dimensional increase over conventional methods. Molecular dynamics and quantum-chemical calculations show that longer-chain alcohols reorganize precursor solvation, while solvent volatility prolongs edge-mediated precursor transport during annealing. This strategy demonstrates universal applicability across diverse organic spacer cations (PEA+, F-PEA+, PentA+), metal centers (Cu2+, Mn2+, Pb2+), and halides (Cl-, Br-, I-). The large lateral dimensions enable direct, solvent-free electrical contact fabrication via physical shadow masking, bypassing chemical degradation from solvents used in conventional lithography. Planar devices fabricated from isolated ultrathin (PEA)2PbI4 channels exhibit ultra-low dark currents down to the 10^-15 - 10^-13 A range, enabling femtowatt-to-picowatt static power consumption, ~ 0.2 pW at 5 V, a 250-fold reduction relative to drop-cast films, while maintaining a high light-to-dark current ratio of 4.3 x 102. This work establishes precise steric and solvation control as a paradigm for scalable, compositionally diverse, low-static-power monolayer 2D perovskite optoelectronics.

infographic.key_insight: Steric and solvation control enables hybrid perovskite monolayers exceeding 1000 µm² in lateral area, supporting lithography-free, low-static-power optoelectronics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Large ultrathin crystals permit solvent-free contacts through physical shadow masks, avoiding solvent-induced degradation during conventional lithography.
method: Use a ternary-solvent strategy combining alcohol cosolvents and an amine additive to suppress out-of-plane stacking.
Tune precursor solvation and solvent volatility to sustain edge-mediated growth during annealing.
Fabricate planar devices from isolated ultrathin (PEA)₂PbI₄ channels using shadow-mask contacts.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports (PEA)₂CuCl₄ monolayers exceeding 1000 µm² and (PEA)₂PbI₄ devices with dark currents of 10⁻¹⁵–10⁻¹³ A, approximately 0.2 pW static power at 5 V, and a light-to-dark current ratio of 430.
infographic.watch_item: Scalable manufacturing still requires validation of monolayer yield, device-to-device uniformity, and long-term operational stability.

title: Interplay of Chemical Disorder, Vortex Pinning, and Electron Correlations in the Mechanically Robust Medium-Entropy Alloy Superconductor $\text{Nb}_{0.45}\text{Ta}_{0.25}\text{Ti}_{0.15}\text{Hf}_{0.15}$
authors: Pooja Chourasia, Samiul Sk, Nikita Sharma, B. Vignolle, Abhishek Sarkar, Olivier Toulemonde
abstract: Medium and high-entropy alloys have emerged as a promising class of superconducting materials because their intrinsic chemical disorder can simultaneously enhance mechanical robustness and modify superconducting properties. Here, we present a combined experimental and first-principles investigation of the structural, superconducting, electronic, and local lattice-distortion characteristics of the mechanically robust medium-entropy alloy $\text{Nb}_{0.45}\text{Ta}_{0.25}\text{Ti}_{0.15}\text{Hf}_{0.15}$. The material shows type-II superconductivity with a transition temperature $T_C^{onset} \approx 7.8 ~\mathrm{K}$. A high critical current density of $J_c = 0.48 \times 10^{6}~\mathrm{A/cm^2}$ is observed, and this is attributed to strong vortex pinning at grain boundaries. Specific-heat analysis indicates a strong electron-phonon coupling ($λ$ = 1.07) with a large isotropic s-wave superconducting gap. Density functional theory calculations explicitly model the intrinsic chemical disorder, predict a stable body-centered cubic phase. These calculations further reveal a metallic electronic structure with substantial Ti- and Ta-derived states at the Fermi level. Additionally, our results quantify a pronounced disorder-induced local lattice distortion ($Δd = 0.086$ A), providing a microscopic basis for the experimentally observed enhanced vortex-pinning landscape. Remarkably, the alloy also exhibits an unusually large Kadowaki-Woods ratio, placing it close to the heavy-fermion regime and indicating enhanced electronic correlations beyond conventional alloy superconductors. Our results demonstrate that entropy-engineered chemical disorder can stabilize robust superconductivity, promote strong flux pinning, and induce correlated electronic behavior, establishing refractory medium-entropy alloys as a promising platform for next-generation superconducting materials.

infographic.key_insight: Chemical disorder in Nb₀.₄₅Ta₀.₂₅Ti₀.₁₅Hf₀.₁₅ supports robust superconductivity, strong vortex pinning, and signatures of enhanced electronic correlations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This mechanically robust medium-entropy alloy offers a promising route toward superconductors that combine current-carrying capability with structural durability.
method: Experimental structural and superconducting characterization.
Specific-heat analysis of pairing and electron–phonon coupling.
Disorder-explicit density functional theory of phase stability, electronic states, and local distortion.

infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify the temperature and magnetic field for the reported critical current density, limiting application-level comparisons.

title: On the Spontaneous Structural Reconstructions of Chalcogen-Depleted MoS$_2$, MoSe$_2$, and Janus MoSSe Monolayers
authors: Bruno Ipaves, Guilherme S. L. Fabris, Raphael B. Oliveira, Pulickel M. Ajayan, Marcelo L. Pereira Junior, Douglas S. Galvão
abstract: Removing one chalcogen layer from a transition-metal dichalcogenide monolayer leaves an undercoordinated sheet that reconstructs as the remaining chalcogen atoms cross the metal plane. Here, we combine \textit{ab initio} and reactive molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of depleted MoS$_2$, MoSe$_2$, and Janus MoSSe, examining each remaining chalcogen on two parent lattices, to show that the remaining chalcogen type determines the structural reconstruction, with only a minor influence from the parent lattice. In \textit{ab initio} trajectories of the Janus-derived sheets, Se crosses the Mo plane already at 300~K, whereas S stays in place at 300~K and the sheet reconstructs only at 900~K. With a free in-plane cell, the crossings precede an anisotropic lattice contraction, which therefore results from the structural reconstruction. Reactive MD simulations of 50~nm sheets show that, when S remains, the Mo lattice stays crystalline in nanometric domains that disappear with time and temperature, with pores/holes at 900~K. In contrast, when Se remains, the Mo lattice loses crystalline order within the first picosecond, and 36--39\% of the Se atoms cross at every temperature. In a depleted lateral MoS$_2$/MoSe$_2$ heterostructure, both modes coexist in one sheet, each half reconstructing like its single-chalcogen counterpart, suggesting chalcogen patterning as a route to define crystalline and disordered regions in a single monolayer.

infographic.key_insight: After one chalcogen layer is removed, the remaining chalcogen—S or Se—primarily determines reconstruction, with only a minor influence from the parent lattice.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Chalcogen patterning could enable crystalline and disordered regions within a single depleted monolayer.
method: Ab initio MD of depleted MoS₂, MoSe₂, and Janus MoSSe derivatives.
Free in-plane cell simulations to resolve reconstruction and lattice contraction.
Reactive MD of 50 nm sheets and a lateral MoS₂/MoSe₂ heterostructure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reactive MD shows Se-retaining sheets lose Mo crystalline order within 1 ps, with 36–39% of Se atoms crossing the Mo plane at every tested temperature, while S-retaining sheets preserve transient crystalline domains.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed patterning route remains simulation-based; experimental control of depletion and reconstruction requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: On the Spontaneous Structural Reconstructions of Chalcogen-Depleted MoS$_2$, MoSe$_2$, and Janus MoSSe Monolayers

title: Thermoelectric properties and modulation doping of ultrawide-bandgap nitride monolayers
authors: Ariel R. Barr
abstract: Two-dimensional III-nitride alloys provide a composition-tunable platform for exploring thermoelectric transport and intrinsic electric-field tolerance. We combine first-principles electronic-structure calculations with semiclassical transport for ordered monolayer B$_{x}$Al$_{1-x}$N and B$_{x}$Ga$_{1-x}$N. State-dependent momentum relaxation times computed with AMSET include acoustic deformation-potential and piezoelectric scattering. Using a common, temperature-independent lattice thermal conductivity of 550 W/mK, we predict maximum thermoelectric figure of merit ZT>2.5 for selected p- and n-type monolayers and ZT>2 at 300~K for n-type B$_{0.25}$Ga$_{0.75}$N. Composition-dependent band curvature, screening, and scattering help interpret the different p- and n-type responses. Vacuum-referenced band alignments identify candidate modulation-doping partners for both carrier types; explicit hGaN/V$_2$O$_5$ calculations yield a hole surface density of approximately 1.6$\times10^{14}$ cm$^{-2}$. A separate phenomenological model using the band gap and maximum phonon frequency predicts intrinsic breakdown fields of 20.06 and 20.74 MVcm for the Al- and Ga-containing x=0.75 alloys, respectively. These results motivate further investigation for thermoelectric and high-field power-electronic applications. The ZT values apply to the specified scattering and lattice-conductivity models, while the breakdown estimates require validation for monolayers and do not resolve field direction.

infographic.key_insight: Composition-tuned III-nitride monolayers show predicted thermoelectric ZT above 2.5 in selected p- and n-type cases, with n-type B₀.₂₅Ga₀.₇₅N exceeding 2 at 300 K.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These monolayers offer candidates for thermoelectric and high-field devices, with band alignments suggesting modulation-doping routes for both carrier types.

title: Folding of Free Polymers Under Confinement by Responsive Hydrogels
authors: Mahesh Aryal, Alan R. Denton
abstract: Controlling the folding of biopolymers in crowded and confined environments, such as the interior of biological cells, remains a significant challenge. Macromolecular crowding and spatial confinement can strongly influence transition pathways between folded and unfolded states of proteins. Such environments can be mimicked in experiments by confining polymers within soft, tunable media, such as hydrogels -- cross-linked polymer networks that swell by absorbing solvent and exhibit stimulus-dependent responsiveness. Here, we develop a self-consistent mean-field theory for the equilibrium swelling and internal composition of a hydrogel immersed in a solution of free polymer coils. The theory extends the Flory-Rehner framework by incorporating free polymer coils, modeled as fluctuating ellipsoids, whose sizes and shapes are characterized by the eigenvalues of the gyration tensor. Confinement of the coils within gel pores is characterized by an effective free-volume fraction, parametrized from numerical calculations for self-avoiding-walk chains between hard walls. Coupled chemical potential equilibrium conditions are solved numerically over ranges of coil molecular weight and free polymer concentration. We find that free polymers drive a non-monotonic swelling response of hydrogels, with osmotic swelling at low concentrations followed by deswelling at higher concentrations, in qualitative agreement with experiment. We further demonstrate that confinement within gel pores reduces the radius of gyration and asphericity of embedded polymer coils, driving them toward compact, globular conformations analogous to folded protein states. These results establish a theoretical foundation for using responsive hydrogels as tunable, artificial chaperone-like systems capable of inducing and controlling biopolymer folding.

infographic.key_insight: A self-consistent theory predicts that responsive hydrogels can compact confined polymer coils into more globular shapes while exhibiting non-monotonic swelling as free-polymer concentration increases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tunable hydrogels could provide artificial chaperone-like environments for controlling biopolymer compaction and potentially folding.
method: Extend Flory–Rehner theory with free polymer coils modeled as fluctuating ellipsoids.
Represent pore confinement using an effective free-volume fraction calibrated to self-avoiding-chain calculations between hard walls.
Numerically solve coupled chemical-potential equilibrium conditions across polymer molecular weights and concentrations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical predictions show swelling followed by deswelling, qualitatively agreeing with experiment, and reduced coil radius of gyration and asphericity under confinement.
infographic.watch_item: The model predicts equilibrium coil compaction, not sequence-specific protein folding or folding kinetics.
infographic.paper_title: Folding of Free Polymers Under Confinement by Responsive Hydrogels

title: Divalent Yb in the Ca$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$ Structure Type: Crystal Growth and Physical Properties of Yb$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$
authors: Midori Amano Patino, Sitaram Ramakrishnan, Davide Donadio, Nils Lamouche, Elise Pachoud, Macha Meplan
abstract: We report on the single-crystal growth, crystal structure, and physical properties of Yb$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$. Single crystal x-ray diffraction shows that the material crystallizes in the Ca$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$ structure-type at ambient conditions, described by orthorhombic symmetry $Pbam$. Magnetization measurements reveal a nearly isotropic diamagnetic response, indicating that Yb is stabilized in a non-magnetic divalent configuration. Electrical resistivity measurements show a metallic behavior. First-principles calculations including spin--orbit coupling describe a metal whose states at the Fermi level are dominated by Bi $6p$ orbitals, with a density of states within 1% of that of the isoelectronic compound Ca$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$, consistent with a filled and chemically inert $4f$ shell. They further show that the nonsymmorphic symmetry of the crystal enforces fourfold-degenerate nodal lines on the Brillouin-zone boundary, four of which cross the Fermi level and give symmetry-enforced Dirac points with a linear transverse dispersion. Despite strong metallic and covalent bonding within the Pd-Bi network, Yb$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$ is realized as a rare-earth analog of the Ca$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$ structure type with divalent Yb ions. This result offers a potential avenue to discover other rare-earth analogs within this structural family.

infographic.key_insight: Yb₃Pd₄Bi₈ is a metallic Ca₃Pd₄Bi₈-type compound with nonmagnetic divalent Yb and predicted symmetry-enforced Dirac points at the Fermi level.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The compound provides a platform for exploring symmetry-protected electronic states and designing rare-earth analogs within this structural family.
method: Single-crystal growth and X-ray structure determination

title: Flexo-Photoresponses from First Principles
authors: Zhichao Guo, Hua Wang, Haowei Xu
abstract: Many functionally important materials, such as silicon, possess high-symmetry crystal structures that forbid even-order nonlinear optical responses, thereby limiting their application in e.g., photonics and optoelectronics. Strain gradients can effectively break symmetries, activating otherwise forbidden optical responses. Although such flexo-photoresponses have attracted considerable interest recently, a comprehensive microscopic theoretical framework is still lacking. Here, we develop a first-principles approach that can systematically evaluate a wide range of flexo-photoresponses in realistic materials. By mapping strain gradients to long-wavelength phonons within the established theory of electron-phonon coupling, our approach captures the nonlocal quantum-mechanical effects of lattice deformations on nonlinear optical responses. Applying the framework to prototypical centrosymmetric materials, including Si, cubic $\rm SrTiO_3$, and monolayer black phosphorus, we demonstrate that a strain gradients of $10^5\sim10^6~\rm m^{-1}$ can induce flexo-second-harmonic generation and flexo-bulk photovoltaic effects comparable to the intrinsic responses of non-centrosymmetric crystals. Our work establishes a rigorous foundation for strain gradient engineering of light-matter interactions, opening new avenues for nanoscale optomechanics, optoelectronics, and beyond.

infographic.key_insight: Strain gradients can break crystal symmetry and activate otherwise forbidden nonlinear optical responses in centrosymmetric materials.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Strain-gradient engineering could enable silicon and other centrosymmetric materials to support nonlinear photonics, optoelectronics, and nanoscale optomechanics.
method: Develop a first-principles framework for flexo-photoresponses.
Map strain gradients to long-wavelength phonons using electron–phonon coupling theory.

infographic.evidence_signal: Calculations for Si, cubic SrTiO3, and monolayer black phosphorus indicate that strain gradients of 10^5–10^6 m⁻¹ can induce second-harmonic generation and bulk photovoltaic responses comparable to intrinsic responses in non-centrosymmetric crystals.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports theoretical predictions; experimentally creating and controlling the required strain gradients remains an implementation concern.
infographic.paper_title: Flexo-Photoresponses from First Principles
